Holding a dialogue key can look like a small input bug and still break the player's understanding of a quest. A report that says “dialogue skips” leaves the next person guessing about focus, repeat events, and the expected interaction. A useful repair task makes those conditions reproducible before anybody asks an agent to change code.

Disclosure: this article was prepared with AI assistance for a Wagglet marketing assignment. The clip is an original, purpose-built browser fixture using scripted keyboard-event flags. It is not footage from a production game or proof of a shipped fix.

## Start with a reproduction someone else can run

The fixture contains five dialogue lines. The original handler advances on every Space keydown, including repeat events. The corrected handler advances on a fresh Space keydown and ignores repeats. Both modes begin on line one.

<video controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;max-width:900px" aria-label="Scripted original and corrected dialogue comparison"><source src="data:video/webm;base64," type="video/webm">Your browser cannot play this WebM. The source download lets you reproduce the comparison.</video>

The recording shows the original reaching “Mission complete,” line five, while the corrected version stays on “Find the brass key,” line two. A single fresh event followed by three repeats drives each comparison. That distinction matters: scripted events exercise the handler's repeat branch; they do not establish how a particular keyboard, mobile wrapper, or accessibility tool produces input.

<p><a download="W-487-repro-source.zip" href="data:application/zip;base64,">Download the complete example source (ZIP)</a></p>

Unzip the source, run `python3 -m http.server 8080` inside its folder, and open `http://localhost:8080`. The fixture needs no package installation. Click **Reset original**, then **Fresh Space** once and **Repeat Space** three times. Reset to the corrected version and repeat that sequence. Its canvas also accepts Space when focused, so a reviewer can separately try a physical held key.

Record the actual environment with the report. This attempt used Chrome 155.0.0.0 on a Mac; the page prints the browser's user-agent string. The canvas is 900 × 360 pixels. This is a local browser check, with no production build, device-performance measurement, or mobile test implied.

## Give the agent a bounded repair brief

The important artifact is the input contract. Here is the fixture's whole transition function:

```js
export function advanceDialogue(index, event, fixed, total = 5) {
  if (event.code !== 'Space') return index;
  if (fixed && event.repeat) return index;
  return Math.min(index + 1, total - 1);
}
```

For a real project, QA should attach the original clip and exact build identifier, name the dialogue route and save state, and explain whether the first press reveals text or advances a line. That last decision belongs to the game's interaction design. It should not emerge accidentally from an agent's first patch.

A paste-ready brief for this fixture is:

> Reproduce the original Space-repeat behavior. Change only the dialogue advancement path so an initial keydown advances one line and repeated keydowns do not advance it again. Keep a second independent press working. Preserve the final-line boundary and unrelated input behavior. Add a focused regression check for these cases. Report changed files and actual commands run. Stop if the real project routes input through a different abstraction or the agreed interaction requires a two-stage reveal.

The narrow scope avoids turning a repeat-event fix into a new input framework. An agent can inspect the existing handler, propose the smallest patch, run the checks available in that checkout, and explain deviations. It cannot infer the studio's desired dialogue rhythm from a stack trace.

## Separate preparation, execution, and acceptance

QA prepares the reproduction, expected behavior, environment, and affected state. The task author adds repository location, relevant files, setup commands, and boundaries. An eligible teammate executes through their own authorized tools and agent session, observes the example, and returns evidence. The feature engineer reviews the input change; QA or the designated feature owner judges the player-facing acceptance criteria.

This is a concrete way to organize **human AI collaboration in game development**. The [Wagglet article on the AI-native mobile game studio stack](https://wagglet.com/blog/ai-native-mobile-game-studio-stack) describes how technical instructions and the human runner's responsibilities travel together. For this example, the useful connection is preserving the reproduction and acceptance boundary across that handoff. The ticket's delivery still needs an independent acceptance decision.

## Require regression proof that matches the claim

Running `node check.mjs` in the supplied source completed these checks locally:

| Input sequence | Original fixture | Corrected fixture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One fresh Space plus three repeats | Line five | Line two |
| Another fresh Space after that | Not the acceptance case | Line three |
| Escape instead of Space | No advancement | No advancement |
| Space at the final line | Bounded at line five | Bounded at line five |

The assertions cover the transition function. The browser comparison covers its connection to the fixture's visible dialogue. Neither establishes integration with a game's input manager. A real repair should repeat the named scenario in the affected build and test focus loss, text reveal, controller navigation, and touch input where those paths exist.

## A short acceptance checklist

- Confirm the clip and report identify the same build and input path.
- Try one physical held key and two separate presses with the dialogue focused.
- Confirm unrelated input and the final line still behave as designed.
- Compare the changed files with the permitted fix scope.
- Attach fresh evidence and record any untested device or input path.

Accept the repair when the evidence satisfies that contract. Keep an untested mobile wrapper or ambiguous reveal rule visible as remaining work. A small bug becomes transferable when another teammate can reproduce it, run a bounded correction, and give the reviewer enough evidence to make a specific decision.
